_note: Frozen content for design review. Taxonomy family — a ruled table of cells, one raised into the accent per page. Dark ground, pale gold. No logos: the subject is kinds of problem, not tools.
brief: The kinds of problem there are, and why the wrong kind gets solved

slots.standfirst: Six categories of problem that look alike from the outside and need completely different responses.
slots.g1: Nobody knows the answer yet. Everything else is premature.
slots.g2: Everybody knows, and two people want different things.
slots.g3: The plan is right and there is nobody free to do it.
slots.g4: It is clear, agreed and possible, and nothing happens.
slots.coverNote: The last page is the category nobody wants to be in

slots.body: Everybody in the room has an opinion and none of them has evidence, so the meeting produces a decision that is really a preference. The only move that helps is a cheap way to find out, and it is almost never the thing on the agenda.
slots.g1: Confident disagreement about a matter of fact.
slots.g2: Escalating to whoever is most senior in the room.
slots.g3: Name the fact, then find the cheapest test of it.
slots.g4: Research that takes longer than acting and learning would.
slots.g5: Somebody changes their mind without losing anything.
slots.g6: Left alone, it becomes a disagreement about people.

slots.body: Explaining harder is the standard response and it never works, because both sides already understand. What is actually in dispute is which cost to accept, and no amount of clarity makes somebody want a different outcome.
slots.g1: The same argument, restated more slowly, twice.
slots.g2: Another deck. Another walkthrough. More detail.
slots.g3: State both costs out loud and pick which one to pay.
slots.g4: A compromise that pays half of each cost and buys neither.
slots.g5: Somebody says what they are giving up, and means it.
slots.g6: Left alone, it goes quiet and comes back at delivery.

slots.body: Everything is agreed, understood and impossible, because the same four people are on every list. Prioritising does not help unless something is genuinely stopped, and a plan with no removals is a wish about how fast people work.
slots.g1: Every item is important and everything is late.
slots.g2: Reordering. It moves the queue without shortening it.
slots.g3: Stop something visibly, so the stop is real.
slots.g4: Hiring, which costs capacity before it adds any.
slots.g5: Somebody has a free week and it is not an accident.
slots.g6: Left alone, it becomes attrition, then a hiring problem.

slots.body: It is clear, agreed and possible, and it does not happen, which reads as a people problem to everybody above it. The honest reading is that doing it costs somebody something and doing nothing costs them nothing.
slots.g1: Reasonable people, agreed plan, no movement at all.
slots.g2: Repeating the request with more urgency in it.
slots.g3: Find who pays and who benefits, then make them the same.
slots.g4: Treating it as a character flaw in whoever is stuck.
slots.g5: It starts moving without anybody being asked again.
slots.g6: Left alone, it becomes a process nobody follows.

slots.body: A question phrased as a choice between two options hides the assumption that those are the options. Restating what has to be true underneath usually dissolves it, and the dissolved version is the only kind that stays solved.
slots.g1: A binary choice that both sides find unsatisfying.
slots.g2: Arguing the two options harder and longer.
slots.g3: Ask what has to be true for either to be right.
slots.g4: Reframing as a way of avoiding a real decision.
slots.g5: The original question stops being interesting.
slots.g6: Left alone, it is re-litigated every quarter forever.

slots.body: Every arrangement worth having produces a specific recurring difficulty, and that difficulty is not a defect to be engineered out. Treating a permanent cost as a temporary failure produces years of solutions to something that was never going away.
slots.g1: The same fix, shipped annually, by different people.
slots.g2: A new system, on the theory the last one was wrong.
slots.g3: Name it as a cost and decide whether it is worth paying.
slots.g4: Calling it a cost when you simply have not tried.
slots.g5: It stops being on the agenda and nothing gets worse.
slots.g6: Left alone, it consumes the budget for real problems.

slots.eyebrow: On the thing that will not move
slots.body: Take whatever has been stuck longest and put it in one of the six. The category rules out most of what has already been tried on it.
slots.g1: You almost always know which one it is immediately.
slots.g2: And it stops the next round of the wrong solution.
slots.closingLine: Nearly every failed fix is the right answer to a category the problem was never in.
slots.signoff: Diagnosis is most of the work
